pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–8 years

- **Topic:** Taking Apart & Rebuilding

- **Standards — US (NGSS 2-PS1-3):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]." Clarification: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3]." DCI PS1.A: "[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3]." SEP: Constructing Explanations. CCC: [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3]."

- **Standards — UK (honest gap):** England's National Curriculum has no direct statutory equivalent — this is a US/NGSS-led idea. It builds on KS1 'objects vs materials' and dovetails with KS1/2 Design & Technology (assembling and reusing components), and it is an early, concrete precursor to the KS2–KS3 idea of conservation of mass (matter persists through rearrangement).

- **Operational details:** Use a small set of pieces (building bricks, magnetic tiles, construction kit) and have children build an object, take it apart, and rebuild the SAME pieces into a different object. Draw attention through observation to the invariant: the pieces themselves are unchanged and none appear or vanish — only their arrangement changes. Count and lay out the pieces before and after to make the persistence visible. Frame it as evidence-gathering ('how do we KNOW the pieces are still the same?') to meet the construct-an-explanation practice. Connect to real reuse (dismantling a Lego model to build a new one; taking apart to recycle) so the idea is grounded in experience. Keep it about a small, countable set of discrete pieces — not yet about invisible particles.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A–B (concrete → early reasoning). The child can take an object apart and rebuild the same pieces into a new object, state that the pieces themselves did not change (only their arrangement), and give evidence (same pieces, same count) that nothing was created or lost — plus an everyday example of reusing pieces to make something new.
bestPractices: Use discrete, countable pieces (bricks, tiles) so 'the pieces still exist' is directly observable and verifiable by counting.
Count and photograph/lay out the pieces before and after so persistence is evidenced, not just asserted — meeting the construct-an-explanation practice.
Emphasise the invariant explicitly: the pieces are unchanged; only the arrangement is different.
Build the SAME pieces into two clearly different objects to show one set of pieces → many possible objects (DCI 'great variety... from a small set').
Ground it in real reuse (rebuilding a Lego model, dismantling for recycling) to connect to children's experience.
Keep the grain at the level of visible pieces — do not jump to invisible particles yet; this is the concrete rehearsal for later conservation ideas.
keyRepresentations: A small set of building bricks / magnetic tiles built into object A, then rebuilt into object B
A before/after piece line-up with a piece count that stays the same
Photos or drawings documenting the same pieces in two arrangements
Real reuse examples (Lego rebuild; flat-pack furniture; recycling depot)
A simple 'same pieces, new object' record sheet
commonMisconceptions: Believing pieces are 'used up', disappear, or are created when an object is taken apart and rebuilt.
Thinking a rebuilt object is made of brand-new material rather than the same pieces rearranged.
Assuming more/bigger arrangements contain more 'stuff' than the pieces they were built from.
Conflating rearrangement with a change to the pieces themselves (the pieces are transformed), rather than only their configuration changing.
Over-extending to substances that are NOT a small set of discrete pieces (e.g. thinking you can un-mix or un-burn things the same way) — this idea is about reversible reassembly of discrete parts.

learn.summary: For ages 7–8, children learn that [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3] taken apart and rebuilt into a different object, with the same pieces persisting — none created or lost, only rearranged (NGSS 2-PS1-3; DCI PS1.A). The core learning move is hands-on: build, disassemble, rebuild a DIFFERENT object from the SAME pieces, and gather evidence (count and lay out pieces before and after) that the set is unchanged. This is a concrete rehearsal for conservation of matter, kept at the level of visible, countable pieces — not invisible particles. Learner construction is emphasised because the standard asks for first-hand observation; recognition/matching and quiz tasks can check the conclusion but do not by themselves let the child perform the take-apart/rebuild or gather the count evidence.

activities.title: Build, take apart, rebuild — same pieces, new object
feedback: If the child says a bigger-looking build 'has more' pieces, re-separate and re-count together; spread the pieces of the smaller build into a long line so 'looks more' is uncoupled from 'is more'.
If the child thinks pieces 'went away' with the first object, hold up the full pile and recount: the arrangement ended, but every piece is still here and could rebuild the original.
Reinforce correct reasoning: 'Yes — same pieces, same count, just arranged differently.'
Prompt for evidence, not just assertion: 'How do we KNOW the pieces are all still here?' — expect counting and one-to-one matching as the answer.
activities.rationale: The standard asks children to construct an evidence-based account through observation; performing the disassemble-and-rebuild themselves and counting the invariant turns the claim into observed evidence rather than an assertion. Building two different objects from one set directly shows the DCI that a great variety of objects comes from a small set of pieces.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-3 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]'; clarification blocks/building bricks; DCI PS1.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3]'; CCC Energy and Matter.
learnerActions: Take a small, countable set of pieces (e.g. 8 building bricks or magnetic tiles) and build one object, such as a robot.
Count every piece in the object, touching each one (or count them before you build), and record the number (e.g. 8). Draw or photograph the pieces so you have a record to check against later.
Take the object fully apart so the pieces are loose and scattered.
Rebuild the SAME pieces into a clearly different object, such as a car.
Count and lay out the pieces again, and compare with your first count: if no piece was dropped, lost or added, the number is the same (8).
Line up the pieces one-to-one against your first count and your drawing or photo of the original pieces to confirm it is the same set — none appeared, none vanished.
Say aloud what changed (the arrangement / the object) and what did not change (the pieces themselves and their count).
activities.intendedInsight: The object can disappear and reappear as something completely new, but not one piece is created or lost — the same small set of pieces is simply rearranged. This is evidence-based: you can count and match the pieces to prove it.

activities.title: One box, two creations challenge
feedback: If the child uses extra or fewer pieces for the second build, pause and recount: the challenge is to use the same set each time.
Celebrate the realisation: 'The same box of pieces made two totally different things!'
activities.rationale: Explicitly building many objects from one set makes the DCI ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3]') concrete and plants the seed of conservation of matter.
sourceClaims: NGSS 2-PS1-3 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 1-LS3-1, 1-PS4-2, 2-PS1-3]'; clarification blocks/building bricks; DCI PS1.A '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-3]'; CCC Energy and Matter.
learnerActions: Starting from one fixed set of pieces, build two different things, one after the other (e.g. a dog, then a car), using every piece each time.
After each build, confirm the piece count is unchanged.
Describe in words or a drawing that both objects came from exactly the same pieces.
activities.intendedInsight: A single small set of pieces can make many different objects — the variety lives in the arrangement, while the set of pieces stays the same.

activities.title: Record and connect to real reuse
feedback: If the child's example involves things that cannot simply be un-made (e.g. paints that have been mixed together, or something that has been burned), gently note that this idea is about reassembling discrete, countable parts — reusing bricks is not the same as trying to undo a paint mixture or a burn.
Affirm good connections: 'Yes — rebuilding Lego uses the same bricks in a new way, just like our build.'
activities.rationale: Grounding the invariant in children's own experience of reuse connects the abstract idea to lived examples and meets the evidence-based reasoning aim; flagging non-reversible cases guards against over-extension.
learnerActions: Photograph or draw the same pieces in both arrangements, with the matching piece count noted for each.
Make a simple 'same pieces, new object' record sheet showing the before and after builds and the equal counts.

Name an everyday example of reusing pieces to make something new — e.g. dismantling a Lego model to build a new one, or taking apart an old toy and using its wheels and screws to build something different.
Explain why that example is the same idea: the pieces are reused, not made from scratch.
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping pieces as pieces and reusing them is something people do in real life; the object changes but the material carries over.

activities.title: Diagnose and discuss: where did the object go?
feedback: If the child gives a different count for the second object, or says pieces 'went away with' the first object, re-separate and re-count together to show the set is intact.
On the reversibility probe, affirm that because all the pieces are still here, the first object could be rebuilt exactly — which shows nothing was lost, only rearranged.

If the child answers 'where did it go?' as if the material itself disappeared, hold up the pile: the arrangement ended but the pieces are all here and could rebuild it — reconnect object versus material.
If two pieces were genuinely removed, help the child see the count really does change now — because pieces were taken away, not because rebuilding destroys pieces.
Reinforce full reasoning: 'Same pieces, same count, new arrangement — the object is an arrangement that can end while the pieces stay.'
activities.rationale: A prediction-before-reveal question forces conservation reasoning rather than after-the-fact agreement, and separating 'where did the object go?' from the material surfaces the object-versus-material distinction. The reversibility probe reinforces that the pieces fully persist, and the pocket variant distinguishes genuine removal of pieces from the mistaken belief that rearranging destroys pieces.
learnerActions: Observe an adult build an object from 10 pieces, take it apart, and build a different object from the very same pieces.
Before the rebuild is re-counted, PREDICT how many pieces the new object has and WHY.
Answer: 'Did any pieces get made or disappear — how do you know?'
Answer: 'Could you build the exact same first object again from these pieces? What does that tell us?'
Answer the deeper question: 'The first object is gone — so where did it go?'
Try the variant: imagine (or watch) two pieces slipped into a pocket before the rebuild — now what is different, and why?
activities.intendedInsight: The count must stay the same because it is the same pieces in a new arrangement. The first object (an arrangement) no longer exists, but every piece (the material) still does — so the original could even be rebuilt. The object ending is not the same as the material vanishing.

constraints: Use discrete, countable pieces (bricks, tiles) so 'the pieces still exist' is directly observable and verifiable by counting.
Count and lay out (or photograph/draw) the pieces before and after so persistence is evidenced, not merely asserted.
Keep the grain at the level of visible pieces — do NOT jump to invisible particles yet; this is concrete rehearsal for later conservation ideas.

This idea is about reversible reassembly of discrete parts. Do not over-extend it to substances that are not a small set of discrete pieces (e.g. un-mixing or un-burning), which do not reverse the same way.

Recognition-only tasks (tapping to match the same piece across two pre-made arrangements, ordering the disassemble→rebuild steps, or a multiple-choice 'did any pieces appear or vanish?') can check the conclusion and surface the 'pieces used up' misconception, but they do not by themselves have the child perform the take-apart/rebuild or gather the piece-count evidence. Use them as checks after hands-on construction, not as a replacement for it.

An in-role dialogue does not itself provide the physical manipulation or elicit the piece-counting observation; it can support discussion and reasoning but does not by itself produce the build-and-count evidence, so pair it with hands-on construction rather than relying on it alone.

England's National Curriculum has no direct statutory equivalent for this specific idea — it is US/NGSS-led, building on KS1 objects-vs-materials and dovetailing with Design & Technology; treat it as a precursor to KS2–KS3 conservation of mass.

Both screen and physical/3D construction can evidence the invariant: physical pieces afford genuine tactile counting and reassembly; a screen model affords a persistent live counter and one-to-one line-up. Choose by available materials and learner needs, not a fixed ranking.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The two cited sources (NGSS 2-PS1-3 page; England National Curriculum PDF) support the standard content and the curriculum-gap framing, not the efficacy of any specific activity format.

The original artefact notes claimed 3D construction 'adds manipulation friction without deepening the invariant' and framed a 2D sandbox as superior; this is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law. Both 2D/screen and physical/3D building can teach the invariant; choose by materials and learner needs, not a universal ranking.

The original claimed a quiz 'checks the conclusion rather than letting the child observe the invariant' and that dialogue 'cannot supply' the insight; these are retained only as scoped affordance limits (recognition does not itself elicit construction; dialogue does not itself elicit the manipulation), not as universal 'only this teaches' claims.

The optional live piece-counter and 'prove it' one-to-one line-up are preserved as concrete feedback mechanisms (whether on paper by counting/matching, or in a screen model), not as mandatory product features.

The playdough prediction task (assessment) tests conservation of amount under reshaping of a continuous material, which is a related but distinct idea from reassembling a countable set of discrete pieces; the prediction-before-reveal move is reused with bricks in Activity 4, and learners should not conclude that squashing playdough is literally 'the same discrete pieces' rearranged — reviewers may wish to clarify this distinction for the age group.

assess.poeTask: Put a ball of playdough on a balance and note the reading. Ask the child to PREDICT whether the number will change if you squash it into ten little balls, and WHY, before you do it. Then reshape and re-weigh: the reading is unchanged. The pre-reshape reason is diagnostic — a conserver predicts 'same, because it's all still there', while a non-conserver predicts more/less and is surprised.
probeDeeper: If I break the car back into a pile, how many bricks now?
Could I build the exact same dog again from these bricks? What does that tell us?
If I slip two bricks into my pocket THEN build the car — now what's different, and why?
Where is the dog now — is it somewhere, or just not built any more?
assess.correctAnswer: Ten bricks (the count is unchanged); no bricks were made or lost — the same pieces were rearranged. The 'dog' as an arrangement no longer exists, but every brick still does.

errorPatterns.pattern: Non-conservation on rearrangement — thinks bricks are gained or lost when the object changes, or that a taller/bigger build 'has more'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-separate and re-count together; if a build looks bigger, spread the other into a line so 'looks more' is uncoupled from 'is more'.
errorPatterns.distractor: The car has more bricks because it's bigger.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a different count for the car, or says some bricks 'went away with the dog'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Object and pieces conflated — 'the dog is destroyed, so its bricks are gone too'; the material is thought to vanish with the object.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Hold up the pile: the dog (the arrangement) has ended, but the bricks (the material) are all here and could rebuild it — reconnect to object-versus-material.
errorPatterns.distractor: The bricks disappeared when the dog was taken apart.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'where did the dog go?' as if the stuff itself disappeared, not just the arrangement.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks pieces are created or destroyed on rebuilding, or a bigger build has more; conflates the object vanishing with the material vanishing.
responseLevels.full: States the pieces still exist and the count is conserved because it's the same pieces rearranged, and transfers the idea (playdough, recycling) — the object is an arrangement that can end while the material persists.
responseLevels.partial: Says the count stays the same for the brick case but doesn't yet generalise that the pieces/material persist regardless of arrangement.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Build a little dog from 10 building bricks in front of the child, then take it apart and build a car from the very same bricks. Ask: 'How many bricks are in the car now? Did any bricks get made or disappear — how do you know?' Then: 'The dog is gone — so where did it go?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The count question forces conservation reasoning. A child who thinks the dog's disappearance means pieces vanished, or that a bigger-looking build 'has more', reveals non-conservation; a conserver says the count must be the same because it's the same pieces in a new arrangement. The tier-2 'where did the dog go?' separates the object (arrangement) from the material (pieces).
